DATA 620 Final Project: Nonprofit Graduate Course Description Analysis using NLP and SNA¶

Abstract¶

Graduate programs in nonprofit management have expanded rapidly alongside the growth and professionalization of the nonprofit sector. Yet, prospective students and employers often lack clear information about what these programs teach or how similarly named programs differ across institutions. Although prior scholarship has raised theoretical concerns about fragmentation in nonprofit education, this study provides the first large-scale empirical examination of linguistic and topical similarity in graduate nonprofit course descriptions.

Drawing on signaling theory, information asymmetry, and catalog-based curriculum research, the study analyzes 616 core course descriptions from 60 U.S. universities offering nonprofit-focused graduate degrees or certificates. The universities are divided across five school types (Business, Public Administration, Social Sciences, Professional Studies, and Other). Using TF–IDF vectorization and cosine similarity, unigram, bigram, and trigram measures, as well as social network analysis, the analysis tests whether curricular heterogeneity exists, how it varies by school type, and how it differs by program title. Results show that course descriptions share a common conceptual foundation, evidenced by recurring core terms and themes, but exhibit substantial linguistic and structural heterogeneity in how these ideas are expressed. Low cosine similarity scores at both the unigram and bigram levels, along with network fragmentation, confirm high variability in phrasing despite thematic overlap, supporting H1a.

Variation is consistent across school types, with uniformly low similarity scores and overlapping vocabularies, supporting H1b. Additionally, although program titles are widely shared across institutions, underlying course descriptions vary considerably, supporting H1c and indicating a disconnect between program naming and curricular content.

These findings demonstrate that nonprofit education operates in a fragmented signaling environment, where programs appear similar through shared terminology but lack consistent communication of substantive differences. This contributes to information asymmetry for students and employers and underscores the need for clearer curricular standardization and signaling mechanisms in nonprofit management education.

Introduction¶

Nonprofit organizations play an indispensable role in modern economies and civil societies, addressing gaps that neither markets nor governments can effectively fill (Brock, 2004). The scope of the nonprofit sector is vast, accounting for nearly ten percent of private-sector employment in the U.S. (United States Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025a). Among private nonprofit workers aged 25 and older, 32.7% held an advanced degree or higher (United States Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025b). This education statistic signals to those interested in the nonprofit industry that formal education is valued. But this raises a question as to what is being valued when the academic infrastructure supporting nonprofit management education has been reported as fragmented (Amey, 1992)? This invites further inquiry into the structure and content of nonprofit management education curricula.

Nonprofit programs are mainly housed in Schools of Public Administration, Schools of Business, Social Science Schools, Schools of Professional Studies, and Other Schools. Each type of school aims to frame nonprofit education differently. However, prospective students, employers, and donors must infer program quality from imperfect signals such as course descriptions, program names, school types, tuition, institutional prestige, and accreditation status, among others. This heterogeneity produces a communication problem, making it challenging to make educational decisions.

From an economic perspective, this is a textbook case of information asymmetry (Akerlof, 1970). This could be problematic, as Akerlof demonstrated that when consumers cannot distinguish between high-quality and low-quality products, markets systematically undervalue genuine quality and reward imitation. In nonprofit management education, the way programs are positioned within institutions serves as a signal, conveying perceived value, credibility, and strategic priority as inputs to calculate whether productive capability will increase and if there is sufficient return. When there are differences between a program's title and the course descriptions that make up that program, it creates information asymmetry and imperfect information.

To address the growing demand for skilled professionals in the nonprofit sector, nonprofit educational programs must be designed to prepare students for critical roles in mission-driven organizations. However, information asymmetry and signal interpretation pose a business problem when schools may not equip students with the skills employers expect. The school type, what it offers, its costs, and even its location may influence how nonprofit education is delivered to meet the needs of the nonprofit sector. Logically, interested employers seeking prospective employees with finance, accounting, and strategic management skills should look for graduates of programs housed in Schools of Business. Interested employers seeking prospective employees with ethics and governance skills should look for graduates of programs housed in Schools of Public Administration. However, with little variation in program titles, nonprofit education experiences are challenging to decipher.

Purpose of the Research¶

The purpose of this research is not solely to detect linguistic heterogeneity but to demonstrate the extent of the problem: a fragmented educational marketplace that confuses students, employers, and accrediting bodies about the meaning of a “nonprofit management” degree. This study is also designed as a diagnostic stage of a longer research agenda that explores how accounting, finance, and auditing frameworks can professionalize nonprofit management education. This paper identifies programmatic structures and course descriptions between school types, and indicates how they communicate value to prospective students and employers.

Main Research Questions¶

  1. How do nonprofit programs vary in course descriptions?
  2. How does school type affect variation in course descriptions?

Hypotheses Development¶

When students explore graduate programs, they make decisions with limited information. As an experience good, they cannot directly observe classroom quality, faculty engagement, or instructional style until they enroll. Instead, they rely on signals such as program titles, course descriptions, costs, and school reputations to decide whether a program aligns with their goals. Course descriptions are curricular design, marketing, and communication, all in one. They inform prospective students about the university's values and the kind of learning experience they can expect.

Faculty, administrators, and staff members write course descriptions and select program titles through professional judgment, committee input, institutional policy, and mimicking other institutions. These choices reflect both academic intent (what faculty want students to learn), and strategic communication (how the program wants to be perceived). Over time, this process creates language that is partly educational and partly symbolic. The language serves as a bridge between what the faculty teach and what students believe they are receiving. When multiple faculty members or departments contribute to a program, their styles and emphases can diverge, resulting in inconsistencies in tone, content, and focus. These differences underlie curricular fragmentation.

Linguistic and topical variation determine how nonprofit education programs signal identity and quality to external audiences. When both are analyzed computationally, they provide a multidimensional framework for detecting fragmentation, coherence, and institutional differentiation in nonprofit curricula. When course descriptions show high variability, they indicate that nonprofit curricula are fragmented in both form and substance. Nonprofit graduate programs are structurally constrained. Regardless of the program, they tend to cover a common core, including leadership, financial management, fundraising, and governance issues. Therefore, the topics should be somewhat similar. Although topics may be similar, they can be expressed through diverse language. The foregoing discussion forms the conceptual foundation for the following hypothesis:

H1a: Course descriptions for nonprofit education programs will demonstrate low topical and high linguistic heterogeneity.

From a signaling perspective, schools borrow similar language and structure to remain competitive and appear credible to external audiences. Universities offering nonprofit management programs rely on a common set of familiar terms, such as "nonprofit", “leadership,” “management,” or “public”. These terms signal legitimacy to external audiences. This creates a shared vocabulary across course descriptions. However, similarity at the level of individual words does not imply similarity in overall meaning. Each program combines these common terms with different topics, emphases, and contextual language. As a result, even though descriptions draw from the same pool of words, they are arranged in distinct ways and paired with different concepts. This produces low cosine similarity and high distinctiveness. Course descriptions overlap in vocabulary, but differ substantially in how that vocabulary is used. In other words, the words may sound familiar, yet remain meaningfully dissimilar when analyzed as complete texts. Fragmentation is adopted by other schools and is not unique to any one type of school. Fragmentation becomes a feature of the broader field of nonprofit education. Therefore, variation is expected across all schools, but its overall magnitude should not differ significantly. This leads to the following hypothesis:

H1b: Course descriptions for nonprofit education programs will demonstrate similar topical and linguistic heterogeneity levels across school types.

Program titles, such as Nonprofit Management, Nonprofit Leadership, or Nonprofit Administration, serve as deliberate identity signals. Faculty and other decision-makers select these names more carefully than course descriptions to communicate the program’s core purpose and target audience. Each program title carries a different meaning. For example, Nonprofit Management may intend to emphasize efficiency, planning, and operations, Nonprofit Leadership may intend to emphasize influence, interpersonal skills, and personal development, and Nonprofit Administration may intend to emphasize governance, policy, and accountability. Students use these program names to interpret what kind of learning experience they will receive. Because each title attracts a different type of student and reflects a different professional logic, it is reasonable to expect greater linguistic and topical variation across program titles than across school types. This leads to the following hypothesis:

H1c: Course descriptions for nonprofit education programs will demonstrate low topical and high linguistic heterogeneity in program names.

Research Design¶

This is a mixed-method qualitative and quantitative study. Data is processed in Python (version 3.13.9), using Jupyter Notebook (version 7.4.5). This analysis requires very complex coding. AI tools are used to assist in the more complex coding. All other guidance is primarily sourced from my originally developed dataset, from Natural Language Toolkit, and Tsvetovat & Kouznetsov (2011). During the Spring/Summer 2025, and Spring 2026 semesters, I manually extracted (copied and pasted into an Excel file) nonprofit graduate-level curricula from publicly accessible web catalogs of 60 U.S. educational institutions offering master’s degrees or certificates in nonprofit education. The educational institutions were identified from the College Navigator website and an internet search of nonprofit curriculum offerings. Each educational institution’s catalog and website were examined. For the purposes of the current research, the collected data included university names, school names, program titles, core versus elective status, and course descriptions. The data was initially recorded in a CSV file in Excel. Feature engineering was employed to create a new variable, “school_type,” and, upon review of the school websites, each school was categorized into one of five school types: Public Administration (PA), Business (B), Social Sciences (S), School of Professional Studies (PS), or Other (O). The dataset currently resides in my GitHub account. AI-assisted tools (ChatGPT) were used to support coding and text refinement. All outputs were reviewed and validated.

I divided the project into modules, as outlined below.

Module 1: Data Setup: List of Libraries Used in this Research.
Module 2: Data Preparation: Load Data.
Module 3: Data Structuring: Subset Columns.
Module 4: Exploratory Data Analysis on Variables.
Module 5: NLTK Analysis.
Module 6: Unigram TF–IDF and Cosine Similarity.
Module 7: Bigram TF-IDF and Cosine Matrix.
Module 8: Linguistic Signal Analysis by School Type.
Module 9: Social Network Analysis: Network Filtering via thresholds.
Module 10: Social Network Analysis: Centrality Measures.
Module 11: Social Network Analysis: Community Detection.

Results and Discussion of Modules¶

The modular analysis provides converging evidence that nonprofit graduate curricula exhibit conceptual convergence and linguistic fragmentation, with important implications for signaling, differentiation, and information asymmetry.

Modules 1–4 cover the structural setup, data import from my GitHub account, data preparation, and structural validation. The original dataset had 22 variables, of which many were not used in this research. Therefore, I subsetted the dataframe to include only the variables of interest. I further subsetted to just core courses and had foregone electives. The rationale for using only core courses is that all students in a program must take them and be exposed to the same general material. Although elective courses are important, they may not provide a uniform experience among students within a program, and leave them for future research. I created a backup copy of the dataset before any transformations. The data was then standardized through text normalization steps, including converting all descriptions to lowercase and removing extraneous whitespace. Deduplication logic was applied. Rows were removed only when they represented exact duplicates within the same university (unitid), program, and course name. This process reduced the dataset from 617 to 616 rows, confirming that only one redundant entry existed. At the same time, 25 duplicate descriptions were intentionally retained, as they represented meaningful reuse across different programs or institutions rather than errors.

In Module Five (5), I began the NLTK Analysis. I removed stopwords obtained from the NLTK library and my own domain-specific word list. The total number of unique stopwords removed from the dataset is 198. I then tokenized the corpus, removed truncated words (a byproduct of copying and pasting from website course descriptions into Excel), and converted them into lists. I then merged all the word lists into a single large list. The total words = 17,385 across 616 documents.

Next, I grouped all of the course descriptions by program_title. The grouping provided some very telling insights into how universities market their nonprofit management programs. There are 42 unique program title names across 60 universities. I created a table that lists each program title and how many times it appears across all universities. A bar chart visually shows the concentration of program titles. Across the 60 universities, there are 35 unique program titles (although many vary only slightly). There are 41 program titles shared by at least 2 universities, with nonprofit management being the most common, shared by 22 universities. This finding supports the need for further investigation to explain why so many universities use the same program titles, yet exploratory data examined thus far suggest that course descriptions differ across nonprofit graduate education programs.

Further inquiry involved a word frequency analysis, specifically a unigram, bigram, and trigram. The unigram analysis showed how often each word appeared across all course descriptions. In a graph, I show the 20 most frequently used words. The five most frequently used words across course descriptions are “nonprofit” (484 occurrences), "course" (408), “organizations” (306), "students" (252), and “management” (250), indicating a strong emphasis on organizations in nonprofit management and the use of academic structural language such as "course" and "students".

A bigram analysis identified frequently used word pairs. The phrase "nonprofit organizations" dominated with 168 appearances, followed by "nonprofit sector" (43), "course provides" (36), and "public administration" (35) times. The bigram analysis revealed the presence of "filler" words, which are generic or non-informative in a course description. I set up code to potentially remove them iteratively until I can be satisfied that no significant filler phrases remain in the analysis.

A trigram analysis identified and captured more context-dependent phrases that make sense only in a specific context. The trigram analysis revealed some meaningful and more filler three-word phrases. The possible meaningful phrases include "human resource management," (12) “public nonprofit organizations,” (12) and “certificate nonprofit management,” (12) indicating an emphasis on organizational management, workforce administration, and academic credentials within the nonprofit sector. In the data, phrases like “topics covered include” and “offers opportunity learn” also appear, which suggest standardized course description language.

To further analyze the words, I used POS Tagging focused on grammatical roles (noun, verb, etc.) to contextually examine how important words are actually used in sentences and whether they are being discussed as ideas or as actions. Over 56% of all words are nouns, focused on ideas and concepts. In contrast, only about 18.6% are verbs, suggesting the courses are described more like academic subjects rather than what students will actually do. Adjectives make up about 21.4% of the language, adding descriptive detail, but much of the structure still follows repetitive patterns that make programs sound similar. Overall, the surprising takeaway is that these programs emphasize what is taught more than how students will apply it.

After POS Tagging, I analyzed word co-occurrence. I selected a small set of keywords from the course descriptions: nonprofit, management, public, and business. I extracted a small window of surrounding words (two before and two after). The resulting phrases are short token-based fragments that illustrate how each word is used. The results indicate that the word "nonprofit" appears primarily in the context of organizations and management. The phrases seem to focus more on real-world organizational structures and not abstract ideas. The word "management" appears primarily as a connector across various areas of management. The phrases seem to focus more on people, functions, and systems. The word "public" appears to be used primarily in the context of government and policy. The phrases seem to focus more on a strong connection to the public sector. The word "business" appears to be used primarily as a descriptor. The phrases seem to focus more on nonprofit programs relative to business education, not as the focus.

In Module Six (6), I shift the analysis to quantify the course descriptions by conducting unigram TF–IDF and cosine similarity analyses. Term Frequency (TF) - Inverse Document Frequency (IDF) assigns a weight to each term within a document based on how informative it is. TF is how often a term appears in a document, and IDF down-weights terms that appear in many documents. A high score means a term is important or distinctive for a document. A low score means a term is common or less important. I analyzed the entire corpus as a single dataset by converting the cleaned text into TF–IDF scores (term importance in documents) to identify the most distinctive terms. I computed unigram cosine similarity between course descriptions, which measures how similar or standardized the language is across all programs. Cosine similarity compares the TF-IDF weights on a scale from 0 to 1. The closer to one, the more similar a course description. Effectively, this part of the research quantifies linguistic distinctiveness and similarity across course descriptions to establish a systematic baseline for assessing variation and standardization.

I analyzed 616 course descriptions across 1,482 terms. The language in the course descriptions is concentrated around a relatively small set of core ideas. The most distinctive terms are **"nonprofit (0.052)," "public (0.043)," "management (0.042)," "course ( 0.040), and "financial" (0.036). They indicate that programs are primarily focused on managing nonprofit organizations within a broader public and social context. The prominence of words like "course," "students," "covers," and "examines" indicates that a significant portion of the language is generic and instructional rather than highly specialized. There are non-generic terms such as "strategies," "planning," "fundraising," and "development", which indicate references to applied skills in the course descriptions. The overall pattern reflects a strong emphasis on conceptual structure and standardized phrasing. The mean TF-IDF scores were low (example: "nonprofit" = 0.052 - the most important term), indicating that course descriptions are largely consistent across programs and show limited differentiation in how content is presented. Note that the scores are not read as percentages, but rather as a ranking. The reported low standard deviation of 0.08 for the word "nonprofit" indicates that words appear similarly across course descriptions.

After quantifying the importance of terms, I computed cosine similarity to show how similar each course description is to the others. The 616 × 616 matrix means every course is compared with all others. The average similarity of 0.039 is very low, indicating that most descriptions differ significantly in their exact wording. A maximum similarity score of 1.0 likely reflects duplicate course descriptions across programs within the same institution. A minimum score of zero reflects total dissimilarity.

In Module Seven (7), I examined bigram TF–IDF and Cosine Similarity analyses. The analysis to this point has focused on unigrams in the overall corpus. However, unigrams are useful for revealing shared isolated words, but lack the rigor that shared phrases could potentially reveal. The bigram analyses identified the most distinctive two-word phrases across the entire corpus. Bigrams may reveal concept-level language rather than isolated words. Each score represents the mean TF–IDF weight of that phrase across all documents. The results show a strong concentration around three thematic clusters. First, the phrases “nonprofit sector,” “public administration,” “public sector,” and “nonprofit management” suggest that the dataset is more focused on nonprofit and government-oriented programs. Second, there is a management and organizational theme surfacing, reflected in phrases such as “financial management,” “strategic planning,” and “human resource.” These suggest that programs emphasize business. Third, there is a mix of instructional and academic language, including “course provides,” “students learn,” “capstone course,” and “research methods.” These are more filler phrases, discussed earlier. They reflect common academic framing rather than domain-specific differentiation.

A bigram cosine similarity analysis showed that at the phrase level across individual course descriptions, they are not similar. The average cosine similarity of 0.006 indicates that course descriptions rarely use the same two-word combinations. In other words, while programs may consistently discuss similar topics such as nonprofit management or public sector work, but they tend to express these ideas using different phrasing, resulting in minimal overlap in bigrams. These results indicate that the dataset is conceptually cohesive but linguistically heterogeneous.

A bigram similarity network showed 616 nodes and 10,437 edges (connections) where institutions share some level of phrase-level similarity. The network is not nearly as dense as the unigram network, meaning many institutions share much less overlapping bigram language in their course descriptions. This suggests that while institutions may differ in specific phrasing, there is still an underlying similarity in how course descriptions are constructed, with recurring phrases appearing across many schools. The fact that the network is not fully dense implies that bigrams are capturing more specific and distinguishing language patterns, which should lead to clearer clustering once weaker edges are filtered out. Like the Unigram Network discussion in Module 6C, applying a threshold will eliminate weak ties.

Module 8 introduces a structured comparison of course descriptions across school types, building on prior evidence that program titles explain very little of the variation in language, as heterogeneity largely occurs within categories. School types are divided by Public Administration (PA), Business (B), Social Sciences (S), Professional Studies (PS), and Other (O). I identified, visualized, and listed universities by school types. I conducted unigram and bigram between-group comparisons. Descriptive results show that PA represents the largest group with 248 observations, B with 191 observations, S and PS, each with 67 observations, while O is the least represented, with 43 observations. Overall, the distribution is uneven, with PA and B comprising the majority of the dataset, while the remaining groups make up a smaller proportion. I included a table to view which universities are in the groupings.

I analyzed Unigram TF–IDF Distinctiveness and Cosine Similarity Between School Types. I identified the most distinctive vocabulary for each school type, computed the mean TF–IDF score for each term in that group, and selected the top 10 highest-scoring terms. terms like “nonprofit,” “management,” and “course” appear across multiple columns as one of the highest three-ranked words. The PA group is strongly associated with “public” (0.072) and “nonprofit” (0.052), which aligns with a public administration focus. PS includes terms like “nonprofit” (0.064), “management” (0.040), and “social” (0.039), suggesting a mix of administrative and social-sector themes. The S group appears to emphasize "nonprofit" (0.052), “course” (0.052) and “organizations” (0.044), pointing toward structural or curricular language rather than domain-specific terminology. The B group shows terms like “nonprofit” (0.049), “course” (0.045), and “management” (0.037), indicating overlap with other groups but with less dominance of any single theme. This overlap, especially around “nonprofit,” “management,” and “course”, suggests shared vocabulary across programs, which may reduce how sharply the groups are separated. Overall, the matrix indicates that S is the most specialized group, O is the most general, and the remaining groups (B, PA, PS) share overlapping terminology with moderate differentiation driven by domain-specific keywords like “public,” “nonprofit,” and “management.”

The results of the Unigram Cosine Similarity Between School Types indicate that course descriptions are highly diverse in their language across all groups. Similarity values are uniformly low, ranging from approximately 0.033 to 0.053, consistent with the overall document-level average and suggesting that most course descriptions share little exact wording. For example, Public Administration (0.044) is only marginally more similar to Business (0.040) or Other programs (0.041). This suggests weak linguistic differentiation across school types. Overall, the findings suggest that while programs share a common baseline vocabulary, the way this language is used varies considerably, limiting the extent to which group membership can be inferred from textual content alone. Phrases like “nonprofit organizations,” “public administration,” and “financial management” appear across multiple columns, indicating common thematic overlap, while other phrases (e.g., “students learn,” “capstone course,” or “strategic planning”) reflect more specialized emphases within particular school types.

I also analyzed Bigram Cosine Similarity Between School Types. The bigram analysis indicates that while school types share a common conceptual foundation, they differ in how that language is emphasized and structured. Core phrases such as “nonprofit organizations,” “public administration,” and “financial management” rank among the top bigrams across groups, with mean TF–IDF values typically ranging from approximately (0.008 to 0.017), indicating consistent importance across the corpus. However, relatively high standard deviations (0.05–0.08) for many of these phrases suggest uneven distribution, meaning they are emphasized more strongly in some programs than others. Pairwise comparisons further show substantial overlap in top-ranked bigrams, particularly between groups such as PA and B, reinforcing a shared conceptual vocabulary. Despite this overlap, cosine similarity scores based on bigram TF–IDF are uniformly very low (approximately 0.002–0.007), with minimal variation between group pairs, indicating that programs rarely use the same two-word phrases in similar ways. The distribution of similarity values, which clusters near zero across all groups, supports this finding. Overall, these results suggest that although programs draw from a shared set of core concepts, differences in phrase-level usage produce weak linguistic similarity across school types.

Module 9 examines a network analysis that adjusts similarity thresholds to reveal how linguistic relationships shift from broad overlap to meaningful separation. The network analysis provides confirmation of these patterns discovered in earlier modules. I calculated the threshold level where the unigram breaks into more than one component, which is 0.1495. I then created a table setting different thresholds at 5%, 10%, 14.95%, 20%, and 40% to illustrate components at different levels. The global unigram threshold at 0.05 still produces a highly connected network (616 nodes, 53,641 edges, 28% density) with a single component, showing that institutions share a widely distributed vocabulary. At 0.10 is still one component. At 0.20, it breaks into 7 components. The bigram threshold at 0.05 is still a single component, but it yields a sparser network (610 nodes, 5,214 edges, 2.8% density), which is then split into two components. This may suggest that shared phrases are far less common. I created a network visualization that shows this contrast. The unigram networks appear as dense, cohesive clusters, while bigram networks are more dispersed, with emerging gaps and smaller groupings. As I increase the unigram threshold to 0.10, the unigram network remains fully connected, but the bigram network fragments into 6 components; by 0.20, this expands to 7 components for unigrams versus 37 for bigrams; and at 0.40, the bigram network breaks into 100 components, revealing highly localized clusters of similarity. Module 9D visually shows this fragmentation, with nodes separating into distinct clusters as weaker ties disappear. Shifting to the group level in Modules 9E–9H, the same pattern persists but becomes even more pronounced. At low thresholds (0.02–0.03), all groups are weakly connected (10 edges), but at 0.04, only 3 edges remain, leaving some groups isolated. Correspondingly, group-level cosine similarities are extremely low (0.002–0.003), indicating minimal shared phrasing across school types. Together, these modules show a clear progression: while general vocabulary creates a densely connected structure, increasing specificity at the phrase level rapidly exposes fragmentation, revealing that linguistic similarity across institutions and groups is weak and not structurally cohesive.

Module 10 examines four centrality measures: degree, closeness, betweenness, and eigenvector, to evaluate how linguistic similarity structures differ between unigram and bigram networks. The results reveal a consistent contrast in the two networks between a dense, homogeneous structure and a sparser, more differentiated network.

In the unigram network, centrality values are uniformly high across all measures, indicating widespread connectivity and minimal differentiation. Degree centrality ranges from 0.56–0.63, showing that most course descriptions are directly connected to a large proportion of others, reflecting extensive overlap in shared vocabulary. Closeness centrality is similarly high (0.69–0.73), indicating that nodes occupy central positions within a tightly integrated network and can reach others through very short paths. Betweenness centrality remains low and relatively uniform (0.004–0.006), suggesting that no nodes play a significant intermediary role. The large amount of redundant connections reduces the need for structural bridges, reinforcing the interpretation of a highly cohesive network. Eigenvector centrality is modest but tightly clustered (0.073–0.084), indicating that influence is evenly distributed across nodes. Because most course descriptions are connected to other highly connected nodes, no single program emerges as structurally dominant. Together, these measures characterize the unigram network as a dense and non-hierarchical network, where similarity is broad, diffuse, and largely undifferentiated.

In the bigram network, centrality values are substantially lower and more variable, indicating a shift toward structural differentiation. Degree centrality drops sharply (0.076–0.091), showing that nodes are directly connected to far fewer others, reflecting limited overlap in phrase-level language. Closeness centrality is also lower (0.43–0.44), indicating greater distance between nodes and a less compact network structure. Betweenness centrality is higher and more variable (0.014–0.023), suggesting that certain nodes act as key bridges connecting otherwise disconnected clusters. These nodes occupy structurally important intermediary positions, linking distinct thematic areas within the dataset. Eigenvector centrality is also more unevenly distributed (0.137–0.167), with a subset of nodes emerging as more influential due to their connections to other highly central nodes. This indicates the presence of a core-periphery structure, in which influence is concentrated among programs that employ widely shared, structurally significant phrase-level combinations, while others remain more peripheral.

Visually, these differences are reflected in network structure: the unigram network forms a dense “hairball,” characterized by extensive overlap and limited separation, whereas the bigram network is sparser, with visible hubs, bridges, and isolated clusters.

Taken together, the centrality measures demonstrate that unigram networks capture broad, generalized similarity, making most programs appear equally central, while bigram networks reveal more selective and meaningful relationships, highlighting fewer but more structurally influential nodes. Unigram centrality reflects commonly used, standardized language across nonprofit programs, whereas bigram centrality identifies where distinctiveness, influence, and thematic integration emerge. These findings indicate that while nonprofit curricula share a common linguistic foundation, meaningful differentiation occurs only at higher levels of linguistic specificity. Influence and structural importance are not evenly distributed across programs but are instead localized within a subset of nodes, supporting the conclusion that differentiation in nonprofit education is fragmented and uneven rather than systemic.

Module 11 examines community detection. The results highlight a critical distinction between broad visibility and meaningful differentiation in nonprofit program positioning. The unigram network produces only 2–3 large, overlapping communities (with two dominant clusters), indicating that most programs cluster and rely on a shared, generalized vocabulary that makes them appear similar. From a strategic perspective, this may suggest that simply using common terms like “nonprofit management” or “social impact” will not meaningfully distinguish a program in a crowded market. In contrast, the bigram network reveals 14 smaller communities, each defined by more specific thematic language such as fundraising, strategic planning, public policy, or financial management. This structure indicates that distinctiveness arises from specific combinations of concepts rather than from individual terms.

However, similar topics fragment into separate clusters due to minor phrasing differences, suggesting that programs lack standardized ways of communicating similar content. As a result, even substantively similar curricula may appear distinct, exacerbating information asymmetry.

Programs that rely on generic language will blend into the large, dense core of the network, making them harder for prospective students to distinguish. In contrast, programs that consistently emphasize specific thematic combinations, such as “grant writing and fundraising,” “public policy and research methods,” or “financial planning and reporting”, are more likely to occupy distinct positions. However, the bigram network produces fragmentation at the margins, where similar financial topics split into multiple small clusters due to minor phrasing differences.

Taken together, the results of the analysis in modules 1-11 provide empirical support for all three hypotheses:

H1a (Heterogeneity): Supported. Course descriptions exhibit clear linguistic and structural heterogeneity, particularly at the phrase level, despite sharing a common conceptual foundation.

H1b (Similarity across school types): Supported. Variation is consistent across institutional categories, with no meaningful differences in the magnitude of heterogeneity between school types.

H1c (Variation by program title): Supported. The widespread reuse of program titles, combined with substantial variation in underlying descriptions, demonstrates that titles function as weak and potentially misleading signals of curricular content.

Limitations¶

Several limitations may affect the analysis. Although catalogs advertise course descriptions, faculty members may deviate in the syllabi. Education is an experience good and can only be truly evaluated after the good is consumed. NLP methods capture patterns but do not fully explain causality, meaning results will be descriptive rather than definitive. Although I took great care in developing the dataset, variation in data completeness or formatting may introduce bias.

Theoretical and Practical Implications¶

From a signaling theory perspective, the findings reveal a decoupling between signal form and signal content. Programs converge on similar labels and core vocabulary to maintain legitimacy, yet diverge in how they articulate substance. This produces a market in which signals are abundant but not discriminative, increasing information asymmetry for students and employers.

From an institutional perspective, the results suggest that nonprofit education has evolved through mimetic processes, adopting shared language without achieving standardization in meaning. The consequence is a fragmented educational marketplace in which apparent similarities mask underlying inconsistencies.

Overall, the evidence indicates that nonprofit graduate education is not lacking in content. It is the coherent, consistent communication of that content that limits the effectiveness of course descriptions as signals of program quality and differentiation.

Module 1: List of Libraries Used in this Research¶

In this module, I provide a list of libraries used to conduct this research. The libraries are repeated inside the subsequent modules so the reader can understand when and how they are used. The libraries give insight to how the analytical approach is framed as a structured NLP and SNA workflow.

In [1]:
# Module 1: List of all unique libraries and submodules used in this research

# Core data handling
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# Text processing/NLP
import re

Module 4: Exploratory Data Analysis on Variables¶

This module checks the structure of the data that there are no missing values, and then looks for patterns, such as repeated course descriptions. The dataset has 617 core course descriptions from 60 different universities. There are 8 variables. The in_state_tuition_course variable needed to be converted from an object to a numeric variable. I also inspected for missing values and found none. The in_state_tuition_course variable is retained in the data set for future analysis.

I identify when the same course content appears multiple times across different programs or universities. Instead of immediately removing those duplicates, I created code to see where the course duplicates occur and how they occur. This is important because those course duplicates are not necessarily errors. They may represent meaningful relationships, like shared curriculum across programs. In this module, I save a clean copy of the original dataset, in case I need to backtrack if something goes wrong in the analyses.

Module 4C: Identify Duplicate Courses¶

This module scans all course descriptions and counts how many times each one appears. It keeps only the descriptions that show up more than once, helping me find courses that are repeated across programs or schools. In simple terms, I am trying to find out which course descriptions are being reused. The result is that 26 course descriptions appear multiple times in my dataset.

In [7]:
# Module 4C: Identify Duplicate Courses

Module 4F: Deduplicate Courses¶

This module simplifies the dataset by removing unnecessary repetition, standardizes the text by removing extra spaces, making everything work lowercase, removing exact duplicate rows, removing courses that have the same name and description, keeping only one version, and resetting the row numbering, and shows the new dataset size. The result shows only 25 duplicate descriptions remain, reducing the dataset from 617 to 616 rows. The means that one (1) row was removed because it was a duplicate or repeated entry within the same program/school and got removed, leaving 25 meaningful duplicates.

In summary, the deduplication process removes duplicate course descriptions in the SAME school, SAME program, but keeps duplicate courses in the SAME school, but a DIFFERENT program, or in a DIFFERENT school, or one with the SAME description, but a DIFFERENT course name. In other words, I am removing repeated courses only when they occur within the same unitid, school, same program, and course name. This structure allows me to analyze how similar course content is offered across programs within the same school as well as across different institutions.

In [10]:
# Module 4F: Deduplicate courses

# Standardize text before deduplication
df['course_desc'] = df['course_desc'].str.strip().str.lower()
df['program_title'] = df['program_title'].str.strip().str.lower()
df['course_name'] = df['course_name'].str.strip().str.lower()

# Remove exact duplicates
df = df.drop_duplicates()

# Remove duplicates based on course meaning
df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=['unitid', 'program_title', 'course_name', 'course_desc'])

# Check duplicates after cleaning
print("Remaining duplicate descriptions:", df['course_desc'].duplicated().sum())

# Reset index
df = df.reset_index(drop=True)

print("Shape after deduplication:", df.shape)

Remaining duplicate descriptions: 25
Shape after deduplication: (616, 8)

Module 4G: Identify shared course descriptions within the same university¶

What this module does is groups data by university (unitid) and course description, then counts how many programs use that course description, and keeps only those used in multiple programs. There are 14 such courses.

In [11]:
# Module 4G: Identify shared course descriptions within the same university

# Count how many programs share each course_desc within each university
shared_courses = df.groupby(['university', 'unitid', 'course_desc'])['program_title'] \
    .nunique() \
    .reset_index(name='num_programs')

# I keep only those used in multiple programs within SAME university
shared_courses = shared_courses[shared_courses['num_programs'] > 1]

# I keep only rows that match valid within-university duplicates
df_within_uni = df.merge(
    shared_courses[['unitid', 'course_desc']],
    on=['unitid', 'course_desc'],
    how='inner'
)

# Verify the result
print("Remaining unique shared courses:",
      df_within_uni[['unitid','course_desc']].drop_duplicates().shape[0])

Remaining unique shared courses: 14

Module 5B: Download stopwords¶

In this module, I downloaded stopwords. The NLTK library contains a tokenizer (“punkt”) and a predefined list of English stopwords. The standard English stopwords include common words such as “the,” “and,” and “is”. These words appear frequently but do not carry meaningful analytical value.

I also included a list of domain-specific stopwords. These are words that may be common within course descriptions, such as “course,” “students,” or “introduction.” In the analysis, I currently commented out the domain-specific stopwords (in effect, placeholders) to include them if needed. The base stopwords and any domain-specific terms are then combined into a single set, creating a comprehensive list of words to exclude from analysis. The total number of stopwords removed from the dataset is 198.

In [15]:
# Module 5B: Download stopwords 

for pkg in ['punkt', 'punkt_tab', 'stopwords']:
    nltk.download(pkg, quiet=True)

# Create stopword lists

# Base stopwords
stop_words = set(stopwords.words('english'))

# Domain-specific stopwords
domain_stopwords = {
    # "course", "students", "introduction", "introduces",
    # "learn", "teaches", "overview", "program",
    # "subject", "field", "education"
}

# Combine
stop_words = stop_words.union(domain_stopwords)

print("Total unique stopwords:", len(stop_words))

Total unique stopwords: 198

Module 5C: Tokenization¶

In this module, I create a function that preprocesses raw text by converting it to lowercase, breaking it into individual words (tokens), and then filtering out unwanted elements. It removes punctuation, numbers, common stop words (like “the” or “and”), and very short words, leaving only meaningful alphabetic terms. Since this corpus came from copying and pasting narrative into Excel cells, truncation and corrupted tokens may exist. In Moducle 5C2. I ran a function to detect any words and "nonprofi" appeared 14 times. In Module 5C3, I corrected the truncations.

In [16]:
# Module 5C1: Tokenization

# Define a function to convert raw text into tokens (tokenization)
 
def preprocess(text):
    tokens = word_tokenize(str(text).lower())
    
    tokens = [
        w for w in tokens
        if w.isalpha()
        and w not in stop_words
        and len(w) > 2
    ]
    return tokens

df['tokens'] = df['course_desc'].apply(preprocess)

# Verify
print('tokens' in df.columns)

True

# Module 5C3: Correct nonprofi truncated words

# "nonprofit" and "nonprofi" token count before correction
all_words_before = [w for row in df['tokens'] for w in row]
counts_before = Counter(all_words_before)

nonprofit_before = counts_before['nonprofit']
nonprofi_before = counts_before['nonprofi']

print("BEFORE FIX")
print("nonprofit:", nonprofit_before)
print("nonprofi :", nonprofi_before)

# Corrected truncated words 
df['tokens'] = df['tokens'].apply(
    lambda row: ['nonprofit' if w == 'nonprofi' else w for w in row]
)

# Token counts after correction
all_words_after = [w for row in df['tokens'] for w in row]
counts_after = Counter(all_words_after)

nonprofit_after = counts_after['nonprofit']
nonprofi_after = counts_after['nonprofi']

print("\nAFTER FIX")
print("nonprofit:", nonprofit_after)
print("nonprofi :", nonprofi_after)

# Validation of corrections

# Ensure truncation removed
assert nonprofi_after == 0, "❌ ERROR: 'nonprofi' still present after fix!"

# Ensure counts increased correctly
expected_after = nonprofit_before + nonprofi_before
assert nonprofit_after == expected_after, (
    f"❌ ERROR: nonprofit count mismatch! Expected {expected_after}, got {nonprofit_after}"
)

Module 5D: Flatten tokens to one large list of words.¶

In this module, I take each course description, clean it, and split it into a list of words (tokens). All numbers are removed, unless spelled out. Then, all those lists are merged into one large list of words. The total words = 17,385 across 616 documents. Once those steps are complete, I can create a word frequency analysis across all courses. For example, the course descriptions "This course examines ethical issues in nonprofit organizations" and "Focuses on financial management in nonprofit organizations" are broken into two lists: ['course', 'examines', 'ethical', 'issues', 'nonprofit', 'organizations'] and ['focuses', 'financial', ['course', 'examines', 'ethical', 'issues', 'nonprofit', 'organizations'] and ['focuses', 'financial', 'management', 'nonprofit', 'organizations']. They are flattened to create one list: ['course', 'examines', 'ethical', 'issues', 'nonprofit', 'organizations', 'focuses', 'financial', 'management', 'nonprofit', 'organizations'].'management', 'nonprofit', 'organizations']. They are flattened into a single list: ['course', 'examines', 'ethical', 'issues', 'nonprofit', 'organizations', 'focuses', 'financial', 'management', 'nonprofit', 'organizations'].

Initial Program Title Analysis¶

Module 5E: Grouped analysis by program_title¶

In this module, I grouped all of the course descriptions by program_title. The grouping provides some very telling insights into how universities market their nonprofit management programs. There are 42 unique program title names. The table below lists each program title and how many times it appears across all universities. A bar chart below visually shows the concentration of program titles.

This module shows that a grouped word-frequency analysis reveals differences in emphasis across program titles, highlighting how institutions frame nonprofit education. Programs such as Nonprofit Management and Nonprofit Administration may be heavily centered on terms like “nonprofit,” “management,” and “organizations,” indicating a strong focus on operational and organizational functions. In contrast, programs incorporating Public Administration may emphasize terms such as “public,” “administration,” and “sector,” reflecting a broader orientation toward governance and policy contexts. Nonprofit Leadership programs may place greater emphasis on leadership-oriented language, including “leadership” and “organizations,” suggesting a focus on strategic and executive development. These patterns demonstrate that, while programs may share a common nonprofit foundation, they could differentiate themselves through distinct thematic priorities in management, leadership, and public-sector engagement.

Here is an example to try to understand this better. I have run these types of scenarios in earlier research, but in this research, I consider them with the updated methodology. Imagine three undergraduate students considering entering a graduate nonprofit program. They all look at course catalogs with very similarly named programs at different universities:

  • Student A is looking at a Nonprofit Management program, which is housed in a Business school.

    • Student A, considering the Nonprofit Management program, more often reads words like: “management,” “organizations,” “financial,” “fundraising”
    • Student A concludes that “This program is about running and managing nonprofit organizations.”

  • Student B is looking at a Nonprofit Management program, which is housed in a Public Administration school.

    • Student B, considering the Public Administration nonprofit program, more often reads words like: “public,” “policy,” “administration,” “sector”
    • Student B concludes that “This program is more about government, policy, and how systems work

  • Student C is looking at a Nonprofit Management program, which is housed in School of Professional Studies school.

    • Student C, considering the Nonprofit Leadership programs, more often reads words like: “leadership,” “strategy,” “development,” “organizations”
    • Student C concludes that “This program focuses on leading organizations and making big decisions.”

General takeaway: Even though all three programs are related to nonprofits, they use different language because they focus on different things. They are all called the same thing, but they differ in their focus on management, public administration, and leadership. It is as if three similar programs speak slightly different dialects of the same language, depending on whether they focus on managing organizations, working in public administration, or leading teams.

Module 5F: Grouped Program Title Analysis Bar Chart¶

This module displays a bar chart of the number of program titles across all course descriptions. The chart shows a highly uneven distribution of program titles across universities, with Nonprofit Management overwhelmingly dominating all others. A small number of closely related programs, such as Nonprofit Administration, Nonprofit Leadership, Nonprofit Management and Leadership, Nonprofit Management and Leadership, form a secondary tier.

For visualization purposes, I collapsed nonprofit management and leadership, and nonprofit leadership and management, into a single nonprofit tier, and collapsed nonprofit leadership (online) into nonprofit leadership. The visualization suggests that, while many programs exist in name, the field is concentrated around a core set of dominant program types, with the remaining universities offering unique program titles, indicating a significant number of niche program titles. Note that 22 are called nonprofit management, 7 are called nonprofit leadership, 6 are called some form of nonprofit management and leadership, 4 are called nonprofit administration, and 2 are called public administration-public and nonprofit management. The remaining names are all unique and appear once.

In [21]:
# Module 5F: Grouped Program Title Analysis Bar Chart

df['program_title_clean'] = df['program_title'].str.lower().str.strip()

df['program_title_clean'] = df['program_title_clean'].replace({
    'nonprofit management and leadership': 'nonprofit management and leadership',
    'nonprofit leadership and management': 'nonprofit management and leadership',
    'nonprofit leadership (online)': 'nonprofit leadership'
})

# Count unique universities per program_title
program_counts = (
    df.groupby('program_title_clean')['university']
    .nunique()
    .sort_values(ascending=True)
)

program_counts = program_counts.tail(5)

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 3))

ax = program_counts.plot(kind='barh')

# Add value labels to the right of each bar
for i, v in enumerate(program_counts):
    ax.text(v + 0.2, i, str(v), va='center')

plt.title("Number of Universities per Program Title")
plt.xlabel("Number of Universities")
plt.ylabel("Program Title")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

df_multi = df_unique[df_unique['program_title_clean'].isin(program_counts.index)]

# Sort data
df_multi = df_multi.sort_values(['program_title_clean', 'university'])

# Group into lists
pivot_dict = (
    df_multi
    .groupby('program_title_clean')['university']
    .apply(list)
    .to_dict()
)

# Create pivot DataFrame
pivot_df = pd.DataFrame(dict([(k, pd.Series(v)) for k, v in pivot_dict.items()]))

# ORDER COLUMNS (descending like visual top → bottom)
ordered_cols = list(program_counts.index[::-1])  # reverse for descending
pivot_df = pivot_df[ordered_cols]

# Final formatting
pivot_df = pivot_df.fillna('').reset_index(drop=True)

# Styling: left-align everything
styled_table = (
    pivot_df.style
    .set_properties(**{'text-align': 'left'})
    .set_table_styles([
        {'selector': 'th', 'props': [('text-align', 'left')]}
    ])
)

Module 5I: Bigram Analysis (2-word phrases)¶

This module shows a bigram analysis. I vet the corpora analyzing bigrams prior to trigrams (3-word combinations) because they are simpler and more general than trigrams. The bigrams help me identify basic, frequently used word pairs that may be generic or non-informative, which I characterize as "filler" phrases. The bigram analysis shows that the most common word pairs. For example, ['nonprofit', 'organizations', 'financial', 'management'] becomes [('nonprofit','organizations'), ('organizations','financial'), ('financial','management')], which may show a focus on managing nonprofit entities and financial management skills. Trigrams, on the other hand, are more context-dependent and may capture phrases that make sense only in a specific context. They require more tokens to form meaningful combinations, making them more complex to analyze and filter at the outset. Only after I conduct a bigram analysis will the trigram analysis be more focused, making it easier to identify more meaningful three-word phrases.

Module 5K: Bigram Filler Phrase Detection and Removal¶

Course descriptions frequently include low-information phrases like "students learn" and "course provides," can artificially inflate similarity and obscure meaningful differentiation. In this module, I identified high-frequency bigrams, which I refer to as filler patterns. They are removed, and I re-run the analysis to distinguish between more marketing-heavy language and signal-relevant language.

In [27]:
# Module 5K: Bigram Filler Phrase Detection and Removal

filler_phrases = set([
    ('nonprofit', 'organizations')
    
])

# Function to remove filler phrases
def remove_filler(tokens):
    cleaned = []
    i = 0
    while i < len(tokens) - 1:  # Loop through the tokens
        # Check if the current token and the next token form a filler phrase
        if (tokens[i], tokens[i+1]) in filler_phrases:
            i += 2  # Skip the next token (i.e., remove the filler phrase)
        else:
            cleaned.append(tokens[i])  # Keep the current token
            i += 1  # Move to the next token
    # Add the last token if it wasn't part of a filler phrase
    if i < len(tokens):
        cleaned.append(tokens[i])
    return cleaned

# Apply the remove_filler function to the tokenized course descriptions
df['tokens_clean'] = df['tokens'].apply(remove_filler)

# Create the cleaned text after filler phrases are removed
df['clean_text'] = df['tokens_clean'].apply(lambda x: " ".join(x))

Module 5P: Trigram Filler Phrase Detection and Removal¶

In [32]:
# Module 5P: Trigram Filler Phrase Detection and Removal

from nltk.util import ngrams
from collections import Counter

# Define filler trigrams
filler_trigrams = set([
    ('must', 'include', 'least'),
    ('paper', 'must', 'include'),
    ('students', 'complete', 'related'),
    ('related', 'checklist', 'found')
])

def remove_filler_trigrams(tokens):
    cleaned = []
    i = 0

    while i < len(tokens) - 2:
        if (tokens[i], tokens[i+1], tokens[i+2]) in filler_trigrams:
            i += 3
        else:
            cleaned.append(tokens[i])
            i += 1

    while i < len(tokens):
        cleaned.append(tokens[i])
        i += 1

    return cleaned

# Apply cleaning of filler phrases
df['tokens_clean_2'] = df['tokens_clean'].apply(remove_filler_trigrams)

# Generate trigrams from cleaned tokens
df['trigrams_clean'] = df['tokens_clean_2'].apply(lambda x: list(ngrams(x, 3)))

# Flatten
all_trigrams = [tg for row in df['trigrams_clean'] for tg in row]

# Count
top_trigrams = Counter(all_trigrams).most_common(50)

print(top_trigrams)

Module 5R: POS (Part-of-Speech) Tagging and Co-occurrence Context Analysis¶

This module contextually examines how important words are actually used in sentences to see whether they are being discussed as ideas (like “nonprofit organization”) or as actions (like “topics covered include”). It shows patterns in language, not what the words actually mean. POS Tagging is focused on grammatical roles (noun, verb, etc.), and co-occurrence refers to which words appear near each other.

Module 5R.1: POS Tagging and Co-occurrence Context Analysis (Corpora as a Whole)¶

Most of the language in these course descriptions focuses on ideas and concepts, not actions. Over 56% of all words are nouns, with common examples like “theory,” “scope,” “functions,” and “sector.” In contrast, only about 18.6% are verbs, and many of those are passive words like “covered” or “including.” This suggests the courses are described more like academic subjects rather than what students will actually do.

Another noticeable pattern is how often the same phrases appear, especially “nonprofit organizations,” which is the most frequent word pair by a wide margin (175 occurrences). Other common pairs like “management + nonprofit” and “public + sector” reinforce that most programs revolve around a few central themes, rather than a wide range of unique topics.

The descriptions also rely heavily on standard, template-like language, which shows up in pairs like “course provides” and “students learn.” Even though adjectives make up about 21.4% of the language, adding descriptive detail, much of the structure still follows repetitive patterns that make programs sound similar.

Overall, the surprising takeaway is that these programs emphasize what is taught more than how students will apply it. Even practical skills like “grant writing,” “human resource,” and “best practices” appear less frequently, suggesting that while hands-on learning exists, it is not the primary focus of how these courses are described.

In [34]:
# Module 5R.1: POS Tagging and Co-occurrence Context Analysis (Answers “How do all the words in the corpora relate?”)

# Apply POS tagging to each tokenized row
from nltk import pos_tag
nltk.download('averaged_perceptron_tagger_eng', quiet=True)
from collections import defaultdict, Counter

df['pos_tags'] = df['tokens'].apply(pos_tag)

# Extract nouns and verbs separately (concept vs action)
def extract_pos(tags, pos_prefix):
    return [word for word, pos in tags if pos.startswith(pos_prefix)]

df['nouns'] = df['pos_tags'].apply(lambda x: extract_pos(x, 'NN'))
df['verbs'] = df['pos_tags'].apply(lambda x: extract_pos(x, 'VB'))

# Flatten all POS tags
all_pos = [pos for row in df['pos_tags'] for (_, pos) in row]

# Count frequencies
pos_counts = Counter(all_pos)

# Group into categories
pos_summary = {
    'Nouns': sum(count for tag, count in pos_counts.items() if tag.startswith('NN')),
    'Verbs': sum(count for tag, count in pos_counts.items() if tag.startswith('VB')),
    'Adjectives': sum(count for tag, count in pos_counts.items() if tag.startswith('JJ')),
    'Adverbs': sum(count for tag, count in pos_counts.items() if tag.startswith('RB')),
}

# Total tokens
total_tokens = sum(pos_counts.values())

# Print summary counts
print("\nPOS Category Summary:")
for category, count in pos_summary.items():
    print(f"{category}: {count}")

# Print percentages
print("\nPOS Distribution (%):")
for category, count in pos_summary.items():
    percent = (count / total_tokens) * 100
    print(f"{category}: {percent:.2f}%")


# Co-occurrence

window_size = 2
co_occurrence = defaultdict(int)

for tokens in df['tokens']:
    for i in range(len(tokens)):
        for j in range(i+1, min(i+window_size+1, len(tokens))):
            pair = tuple(sorted([tokens[i], tokens[j]]))
            co_occurrence[pair] += 1

# Display sample outputs
print("\nSample POS tags:", df['pos_tags'].iloc[0][:10])
print("Top noun examples:", df['nouns'].iloc[0][:10])
print("Top verb examples:", df['verbs'].iloc[0][:10])

# Top co-occurring pairs
top_pairs = sorted(co_occurrence.items(), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)[:20]
print("\nTop co-occurring word pairs:", top_pairs)

Module 5R.2: POS Tagging and Co-occurrence Context Analysis (Using Specific Words)¶

This module examines a small set of key words found in the course descriptions: nonprofit, management, public, and business. The code shows how these keywords are used in context. The code identifies each occurrence of these words and extracts a small window of surrounding words (two before and two after). The resulting phrases are short token-based fragments that illustrate how each word is used, based on preprocessed text where stopwords have been removed, and meaningful bigrams and trigrams have been preserved.

The results indicate that the word "Nonprofit" appears primarily in the context of organizations and management. For example, “nonprofit sector” and “nonprofit management”. The phrases seem to focus more on real-world organizational structures and not abstract ideas.

The results indicate that the word "Management" appears primarily as a connector across various areas of management. For example, “human resource management” and “management staff”. The phrases seem to focus more on people, functions, and systems.

The results indicate that the word "Public" appears to be used primarily in the context of government and policy. For example, “public administration” and “public policy”. The phrases seem to focus more on a strong connection to the public sector.

The results indicate that the word "Business" appears to be used primarily as a descriptor. For example, “business management” and “business graduates”. The phrases seem to focus more on nonprofit programs relative to business education, not as the focus.

In [35]:
# Module 5R.2: POS Tagging and Co-occurrence Context Analysis (Answers “How are the target words in the list below used?”)

nltk.download('averaged_perceptron_tagger', quiet=True)
nltk.download('averaged_perceptron_tagger_eng', quiet=True)  # If 'averaged_perceptron_tagger' doesn't resolve the issue
from nltk import pos_tag
from collections import defaultdict

# Target words
target_words = ['nonprofit', 'management', 'public', 'business']

df['pos_tags'] = df['tokens_clean_2'].apply(pos_tag)

# Context storage
context_dict = defaultdict(list)

window_size = 2

for tokens in df['tokens_clean_2']:
    for i, word in enumerate(tokens):
        if word in target_words:
            left = tokens[max(0, i - window_size):i]
            right = tokens[i + 1:i + 1 + window_size]
            context = left + [word] + right
            context_dict[word].append(" ".join(context))

# Display results
for word, contexts in context_dict.items():
    print(f"\n{word.upper()} (sample contexts):\n")
    for c in contexts[:5]:
        print("-", c)

Module 6: Unigram TF–IDF + Cosine Similarity¶

Module 6A: Unigram TF–IDF Distinctiveness¶

This module analyzed 616 course descriptions across 1,482 terms. It shows that the language in the course descriptions is concentrated around a relatively small set of core ideas. The most distinctive terms are "nonprofit," "public," "management," "financial," and "leadership". They indicate that programs are primarily focused on managing nonprofit organizations within a broader public and social context. The prominence of words like "course," "students," "covers," and "examines" indicates that a significant portion of the language is generic and instructional rather than highly specialized. There are non-generic terms such as "strategies," "planning," "fundraising," and "development", which indicate references to applied skills in the course descriptions. The overall pattern reflects a strong emphasis on conceptual structure and standardized phrasing.

The low TF-IDF scores indicate that course descriptions are largely consistent across programs, with limited differentiation in how content is presented. The reported low standard deviation scores of 0.10 or less indicate that words appear uneven across course descriptions.

In [36]:
# Module 6A: Unigram TF–IDF Distinctiveness

from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
import pandas as pd

# Build corpus
docs = df['tokens_clean_2'].apply(lambda x: " ".join(x))

# TF–IDF
vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer(
    lowercase=False,
    tokenizer=lambda x: x.split(),
    preprocessor=None,
    token_pattern=None,
    min_df=2
)

tfidf_matrix = vectorizer.fit_transform(docs)

tfidf_df = pd.DataFrame(
    tfidf_matrix.toarray(),
    columns=vectorizer.get_feature_names_out()
)

print("TF-IDF matrix shape:", tfidf_df.shape)

# Mean and Standard Deviation
summary_uni = pd.DataFrame({
    'mean': tfidf_df.mean(axis=0),
    'std': tfidf_df.std(axis=0)
})

# Top 20 terms by mean
top_terms = summary_uni.sort_values(by='mean', ascending=False).head(20)

print("\nTop Unigram Terms (Mean + Std):\n")
print(top_terms.round(3))

Module 6B: Unigram Cosine Similarity¶

This module shows the unigram cosine similarity results and how similar each course description is to the others. The 616 × 616 matrix means every course is compared with all others. The average similarity of 0.039 is very low, indicating that most descriptions differ significantly in their exact wording. For example, one course might say “financial management and strategic planning in nonprofit organizations,” while another says “resource development and budgeting for social sector agencies.” These describe similar ideas but use different language, resulting in low similarity scores.

The maximum similarity score of 1.0 likely reflects duplicate course descriptions across programs within the same institution, as discussed earlier. This reuse of course descriptions results in perfect similarity scores, indicating that the overlap is structural (shared courses) rather than conceptual similarity across different institutions.

In [37]:
# Module 6B: Unigram Cosine Similarity 

from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

tfidf_matrix = vectorizer.fit_transform(docs)
cosine_matrix = cosine_similarity(tfidf_matrix)

cosine_df = pd.DataFrame(
    cosine_matrix,
    index=df.index,
    columns=df.index
)

print("\nCosine similarity matrix shape:", cosine_df.shape)

# Summary Metrics

np.fill_diagonal(cosine_matrix, np.nan)

print("\nAverage similarity:", round(np.nanmean(cosine_matrix), 3))
print("Max similarity:", round(np.nanmax(cosine_matrix), 3))
print("Min similarity:", round(np.nanmin(cosine_matrix), 3))

Module 6C: Convert Similarity Matrix to Network Graph for Later SNA Analysis¶

Module 6C converts the cosine similarity matrix into a network structure. Then it can later be analyzed using social network analysis methods. Each institution becomes a node, and the similarity scores between them become weighted connections (edges), allowing the relationships to be studied as a system rather than as isolated pairwise comparisons. This enables the analysis to move beyond simple similarity scores and into structural insights such as influence and connectivity. It shows a unigram similarity network with 616 nodes and 117,515 edges (connections), in which institutions share some level of word-level similarity. This network is dense, meaning most institutions are connected to many others based on shared vocabulary in their course descriptions. Compared to a fully connected network (which would have (616 × 615) / 2 = 189,420 edges), this indicates that unigram similarity captures a very broad level of overlap. This means many institutions appear similar when viewed solely at the level of individual words, because common terms are widely used across course descriptions.

Unigram analysis tends to emphasize general, shared language rather than distinct phrasing. As a result, the network includes a large number of connections, many of which are relatively weak or generic. From an SNA perspective, this makes it difficult to immediately identify meaningful structure, such as clear clusters because everything is so interconnected. The network analysis will later need to apply a threshold to remove weaker connections. As weaker ties are filtered out, the network should begin to separate into smaller, more meaningful groups, helping to reveal which institutions are truly similar in their use of language and which are only loosely connected through common, generic terms.

In [38]:
# Module 6C: Convert Similarity Matrix to Network Graph for Later SNA Analysis

import networkx as nx

G_uni = nx.from_pandas_adjacency(cosine_df)
G_uni.remove_edges_from(nx.selfloop_edges(G_uni))

print("Unigram network:")
print("Nodes:", G_uni.number_of_nodes())
print("Edges:", G_uni.number_of_edges())

Module 7: Bigram TF-IDF + Cosine Matrix¶

Module 7A: BigramTF–IDF Distinctiveness¶

Module 7A identifies the most distinctive two-word phrases (bigrams) across the entire corpus. Bigrams may reveal concept-level language rather than isolated words. Each score represents the mean TF–IDF weight of that phrase across all documents. Higher values indicate phrases that are both frequent within documents and discriminative across the corpus. The results show a strong concentration around three thematic clusters. First, the phrases “nonprofit sector,” “public administration,” “public sector,” and “nonprofit management” suggest that the dataset is more focused on nonprofit and government-oriented programs. Second, there is a management and organizational theme surfacing, reflected in phrases such as “financial management,” “strategic planning,” and “human resource.” These suggest that programs emphasize business. Third, there is a mix of instructional and academic language, including “course provides,” “students learn,” “capstone course,” and “research methods.” These are more filler phrases, discussed earlier. They reflect common academic framing rather than domain-specific differentiation.

The reported low standard deviation scores of 0.08 or less indicate that phrases appear uneven across course descriptions.

In [39]:

)

)

    'mean': tfidf_df_bg.mean(axis=0),

})

# Top 20 by mean
top_bigrams = summary_bg.sort_values(by='mean', ascending=False).head(20)

Module 7B: Bigram Cosine Similarity¶

Module 7B examines bigram cosine similarity analysis to see if shared themes translate into similarity at the phrase level across individual course descriptions. The results suggest that they are not similar. Despite the presence of common thematic clusters, the average cosine similarity of 0.006 indicates that course descriptions rarely use the same two-word combinations. In other words, while programs may consistently discuss similar topics such as nonprofit management or public sector work, they tend to express these ideas using different phrasing, resulting in minimal overlap in bigrams. These results indicate that the dataset is conceptually cohesive but linguistically heterogeneous. Course descriptons align in subject matter but diverge in how they articulate those concepts.

Module 7C: Convert Bigram Similarity Matrix to Network Graph for Later SNA Analysis¶

Module 7C shows a bigram similarity network that contains 616 nodes and 10,481 edges (connections) where institutions share some level of phrase-level similarity. The network is not nearly as dense as the unigram network, meaning many institutions share much less overlapping bigram language in their course descriptions. Bigrams are more selective than unigrams. This suggests that while institutions may differ in specific phrasing, there is still an underlying similarity in how course descriptions are constructed, with recurring phrases appearing across many schools. The fact that the network is not fully dense implies that bigrams are capturing more specific and distinguishing language patterns, which should lead to clearer clustering once weaker edges are filtered out. Like the Unigram Network discussion in Module 6C, applying a threshold will eliminate weak ties.

Module 8: Linguistic Signal Analysis by School Type¶

This module introduces a structured comparison of course descriptions across school types, building on prior evidence that program titles explain very little of the variation in language, while heterogeneity largely occurs within categories. The school types are divided by Public Administration (PA), Business (B), Social Sciences (S), Professional Studies (PS), and Other (O).

By segmenting the dataset by school_type, this module explores whether institutional context produces more meaningful linguistic distinctions than program titles. I examined between-group differences to gain further insight. Modules 8A1-3 identification, visualizes, and lists Universities by School Types. Modules 8B1-6 explore Unigram between-group insights. Modules 8C1-6 explores bigram between-group insights.

Module 8A1: Identification and Distribution of School Types¶

Public Administration (PA) represents the largest group with 248 observations, followed by Business (B) with 191. Smaller groups include S and PS, each with 67 observations, while O is the least represented, with 43 observations. Overall, the distribution is uneven, with PA and B comprising the majority of the dataset, while the remaining groups make up a smaller proportion.
